title: Given a Scenario, Select and Configure Wireless Devices and Technologies

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Wireless design requires more than an SSID and password. Learn to select spectrum, plan channels, identify service sets, choose a topology, secure access, shape coverage, and manage access points.

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: Given a wireless deployment, choose the appropriate frequency, channel design, network type, security method, antenna, and AP architecture.
bullets: Spectrum used by a channel → Channel width
Longer reach and wall penetration → 2.4 GHz
More capacity and less legacy interference → 5 GHz
Move capable clients toward a preferred band → Band steering

entries.title: Wireless Channels
paragraphs: Wireless frequencies are divided into channels—lanes in the wireless spectrum. Good channel planning reduces interference and improves performance.

entries.title: Channel Width
paragraphs: Channel width is how much spectrum a channel occupies. Wider channels can increase potential throughput, but they consume more spectrum and can reduce the number of usable non-overlapping channels.
entries.memoryHook: How wide is the wireless lane?

entries.title: Non-Overlapping Channels
paragraphs: Overlapping frequency ranges can interfere. Assigning non-overlapping channels to nearby APs keeps neighboring WLAN cells from talking over one another.
entries.recognitionCue: Nearby APs need interference-minimizing assignments → Non-overlapping channels.

entries.title: Regulatory Impacts and 802.11h
paragraphs: Regional rules can govern allowed channels, transmit power, and frequency behavior. 802.11h provides regulatory and coexistence mechanisms for portions of the 5 GHz spectrum, including radar-related concerns.

sections.title: Frequency Options and Band Steering

entries.title: 2.4 GHz
paragraphs: 2.4 GHz generally offers greater range and better obstacle penetration than higher frequencies, but has less spectrum and commonly more interference.

entries.title: 5 GHz
paragraphs: 5 GHz provides more spectrum and channel options and often less legacy interference than 2.4 GHz. Its practical reach and penetration are generally lower.

entries.title: 6 GHz
paragraphs: 6 GHz adds newer spectrum for compatible Wi-Fi devices and access points. Compatibility is essential.

entries.title: Band Steering
paragraphs: Band steering encourages capable clients toward a preferred band, helping distribute clients away from congestion.
entries.memoryHook: Move capable clients to the better band.

sections.callout: Reach → 2.4 GHz. Capacity → 5 GHz. New spectrum → 6 GHz.

sections.title: SSID, BSSID, and ESSID

entries.title: Service Set Identifier (SSID)
paragraphs: The SSID is the human-recognizable wireless network name users select, such as GSA-WiFi.

entries.title: Basic Service Set Identifier (BSSID)
paragraphs: The BSSID identifies a specific basic service set, commonly a particular AP radio interface. It distinguishes which radio a client is using.

entries.title: Extended Service Set Identifier (ESSID)
paragraphs: An extended service set lets multiple APs participate in a broader WLAN with a common network identity and roaming coverage.

sections.callout: Name → SSID. Specific AP → BSSID. Extended multi-AP WLAN → ESSID.

entries.title: Mesh Networks
paragraphs: Wireless mesh nodes interconnect and can forward traffic through multiple wireless paths.
entries.memoryHook: Wireless nodes connect to one another.

entries.title: Ad Hoc
paragraphs: Devices communicate directly without a traditional access point.

entries.title: Point-to-Point
paragraphs: A point-to-point wireless link bridges exactly two locations. Directional antennas are commonly appropriate.

entries.title: Infrastructure
paragraphs: In infrastructure mode, clients connect through an access point to reach network resources.

sections.title: Wireless Encryption

entries.title: Wi-Fi Protected Access 2 (WPA2)
paragraphs: WPA2 is the established, widely deployed secure Wi-Fi generation that preceded WPA3.

entries.title: WPA3
paragraphs: WPA3 is the newer Wi-Fi security generation and improves wireless security when supported by the AP and clients.

sections.callout: WPA2 and WPA3 describe security generations; PSK and Enterprise describe authentication models.

sections.title: Guest Access and Authentication

entries.title: Guest Networks
paragraphs: A guest network gives visitors access while separating them from trusted internal resources.

entries.title: Captive Portals
paragraphs: A captive portal redirects a newly connected user to a web page for login, registration, an access code, or terms acceptance before normal access is granted.
entries.memoryHook: Connect to Wi-Fi, then a web page appears.

entries.title: Pre-Shared Key (PSK)
paragraphs: PSK authentication uses one shared wireless credential. It is simple, but becomes difficult to manage securely at organizational scale.
entries.memoryHook: Everyone knows the same Wi-Fi password.

entries.title: Enterprise Authentication
paragraphs: Enterprise authentication provides centrally managed, individual identities instead of one shared password. It is appropriate where stronger identity and access control are required.

sections.callout: A guest network can use a captive portal, but they are not the same. Shared credential → PSK. Individual identity → Enterprise.

sections.title: Omnidirectional and Directional Antennas

entries.title: Omnidirectional
paragraphs: An omnidirectional antenna spreads coverage broadly around the antenna and suits clients located in many directions.

entries.title: Directional
paragraphs: A directional antenna focuses radio energy toward a chosen direction. It suits focused coverage and point-to-point building links.

sections.callout: Broad surrounding coverage → Omnidirectional. Focused coverage → Directional.

entries.title: Autonomous AP
paragraphs: An autonomous AP operates and is configured largely as an independent device. Individual management can fit a small environment.

entries.title: Lightweight AP
paragraphs: A lightweight AP relies on centralized management or control, simplifying larger deployments with many APs.
entries.memoryHook: A central controller manages the APs.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Spectrum consumed by a channel → Channel width
Move clients between bands → Band steering
Web page before access → Captive portal

entries.title: Channel Width vs. Channel
paragraphs: Channel → Frequency allocation in use. Channel width → Amount of spectrum the channel occupies.

entries.title: 2.4 GHz vs. 5 GHz vs. 6 GHz
paragraphs: Range and penetration → 2.4 GHz. More spectrum and capacity → 5 GHz. Additional newer spectrum → 6 GHz.

entries.title: SSID vs. BSSID
paragraphs: Network name users recognize → SSID. Specific AP/radio identity → BSSID.

entries.title: Ad Hoc vs. Infrastructure
paragraphs: Devices communicate directly → Ad hoc. Clients connect through an AP → Infrastructure.

entries.title: Mesh vs. Point-to-Point
paragraphs: Multiple interconnected wireless nodes → Mesh. Exactly two locations → Point-to-point.

entries.title: WPA3 vs. Enterprise
paragraphs: WPA3 is a wireless security generation. Enterprise is an authentication model.

entries.title: PSK vs. Enterprise
paragraphs: Shared credential → PSK. Individual central authentication → Enterprise.

entries.title: Guest Network vs. Captive Portal
paragraphs: Separate visitor network → Guest network. Web interaction before access → Captive portal.

entries.title: Omnidirectional vs. Directional
paragraphs: Broad coverage → Omnidirectional. Focused coverage → Directional.

entries.title: Autonomous vs. Lightweight
paragraphs: Independently managed → Autonomous. Centrally managed → Lightweight.
